content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued updated guidelines for the treatment of visceral leishmaniasis (VL) in patients co-infected with HIV in East Africa and South-East Asia. These guidelines are based on recent clinical evidence and aim to address the unique challenges posed by the co-infection, which significantly complicates disease management and increases the risk of poor outcomes. Visceral leishmaniasis, caused by Leishmania donovani, is a neglected tropical disease transmitted by the bites of female sandflies. It disproportionately affects marginalized populations with limited access to healthcare. When co-infected with HIV, patients experience a mutual reinforcement of the two diseases, leading to severe immune suppression, higher parasite loads, increased drug toxicity, frequent relapses, and higher mortality rates. This co-infection also poses a public health challenge, as co-infected individuals are highly infectious to sandflies, increasing the risk of disease transmission. The guidelines recommend combination therapy with liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB) and miltefosine as the preferred treatment for VL in HIV co-infected patients. In East Africa, the regimen involves L-AmB (up to a total of 30 mg/kg, administered on days 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, and 11) combined with miltefosine (100 mg/day for 28 days). In South-East Asia, the same L-AmB regimen is combined with miltefosine for 14 days. These recommendations are conditional and based on very low-certainty evidence, reflecting the limited data available from high-burden regions. For patients who do not respond well to initial treatment, extended therapy or repeated regimens may be considered, particularly in East Africa, where evidence supports this approach. If miltefosine is unavailable, monotherapy with L-AmB (up to a total of 40 mg/kg) is an alternative option. Comprehensive clinical management, including antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV, nutritional support, and access to contraception and pregnancy testing for women of childbearing potential, is essential. Secondary prophylaxis is recommended for patients at high risk of relapse, such as those with low CD4 cell counts (<200 cells/mm³) or multiple previous VL episodes. In East Africa, pentamidine isethionate (4 mg/kg every 3–4 weeks) is suggested, while in South-East Asia, amphotericin B deoxycholate (1 mg/kg every 3–4 weeks) or L-AmB (3–5 mg/kg every 3–4 weeks) may be used. Prophylaxis can be discontinued if the patient maintains a CD4 count of ≥350 cells/mm³ or achieves an undetectable HIV viral load for at least six months without clinical evidence of VL relapse. The guidelines emphasize the importance of routine HIV testing for all VL patients and tuberculosis screening at diagnosis and follow-up. Addressing the challenges of VL-HIV co-infection requires integrated approaches aligned with WHO’s roadmap for neglected tropical diseases and the Sustainable Development Goals. These recommendations are intended for use by national leishmaniasis control program managers, policymakers, clinicians, and other stakeholders involved in the management of VL and HIV. The guidelines aim to provide evidence-based therapeutic options tailored to the epidemiological, clinical, and operational contexts of East Africa and South-East Asia, while promoting equity, human rights, and gender equality in healthcare delivery.
